name: Poetic licence (ḍarūra)
definition: What a poet may do for the sake of metre or rhyme that is not allowed in prose: adding or dropping tanwīn, lengthening or shortening a vowel, changing the order of words.
body: The grammarians kept a list of the licences of verse (ḍarāʾir al-shiʿr); Ibn ʿUṣfūr wrote a book of them. A counterexample from poetry is often answered 'this is a ḍarūra', which saves the rule for prose. The two schools disagreed over how far the licence goes: the Kufans allowed, for instance, a diptote to be made a triptote in verse more freely than the Basrans, and al-Inṣāf records several such questions.
The best-known example in the books is the line of Imruʾ al-Qays in which the woman's name ʿUnayza, a diptote, takes tanwīn for the metre.

examples.text: Imruʾ al-Qays: ʿunayzatin with tanwīn, which a woman's name does not take in prose: a ḍarūra of verse.
